content: Genital ulcer disease (GUD) can increase the risk of acquiring HIV due to the disruption of mucosal surfaces, which facilitates viral entry. Treating GUD and resolving the ulcers may potentially reduce the risk of sexual acquisition of HIV. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of GUD treatment on the likelihood of acquiring HIV through sexual transmission. To investigate this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, EMBASE, LILACS, NLM Gateway, Web of Science, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, ClinicalTrials.gov, and reference lists of relevant publications. The search included studies published between 1980 and August 2011. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, specifically those that compared any treatment for GUD with an alternative treatment, placebo, or no treatment. The trials had to randomize individuals with confirmed GUD as the unit of analysis. Data from the selected studies were independently extracted and analyzed by multiple reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion and arbitration. The results of the studies were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Three RCTs met the inclusion criteria. These trials included HIV-negative participants with either chancroid (two trials, 143 participants) or primary syphilis (one trial, 30 participants). The syphilis study, conducted in the United States between 1995 and 1997, compared three treatment regimens: a single 2.0 g oral dose of azithromycin (11 participants), two 2.0 g oral doses of azithromycin given six to eight days apart (eight participants), and benzathine penicillin G administered as a 2.4 million-unit intramuscular injection either once or twice seven days apart (11 participants). None of the participants in this trial seroconverted to HIV during the 12-month follow-up period. The chancroid trials, conducted in Kenya by 1990, compared different treatment regimens. One trial (45 participants) compared a single 400 mg oral dose of fleroxacin with a 200 mg dose of fleroxacin, finding no significant difference in HIV seroconversion rates (RR 3.00; 95% CI 0.29 to 30.69). Another trial (98 participants) compared 400 mg fleroxacin with a combination of 800 mg sulfamethoxazole and 160 mg trimethoprim, also finding no significant difference in HIV seroconversion rates (RR 0.33; 95% CI 0.04 to 3.09). Adverse events reported in these trials were mild to moderate, including Jarisch-Herxheimer reactions and gastrointestinal symptoms, with no significant differences in the incidence of adverse events between treatment groups. The quality of evidence regarding the effectiveness of GUD treatment in reducing the risk of HIV acquisition was assessed as very low using the GRADE methodology. This indicates that the true effect of GUD treatment on HIV acquisition may differ substantially from the estimates derived from the available data. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether treating GUD reduces the risk of acquiring HIV through sexual transmission. The very low quality of the evidence highlights the need for further research. However, GUD remains a significant public health issue, and individuals with these conditions should receive appropriate treatment, regardless of its potential impact on HIV risk.
